edits.english: MISHNA: With regard to a gentile who was transporting barrels of wine from one place to another place together with a Jew, if the wine was under the presumption of being supervised, it is permitted. But if the Jew notified the gentile that the Jew was going far away, the wine is forbidden if the Jew left for a sufficient amount of time for the gentile to bore a hole [sheyishtom] in the barrel, seal the barrel again with plaster, and for the plaster to dry. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: The wine is forbidden only if it was sufficient time for the gentile to open the barrel by removing the stopper altogether, stop the barrel again by making a new stopper, and for the new stopper to dry.

If it was under the presumption of being supervised - The Gemara explains that even though the Jew went far away from the gentile by a mil, if the Jew did not inform the gentile that the Jew was going far away, the wine is permitted, because the gentile is always afraid that the Jew might come now.
And if he notified him that he was going far away - that the Jew was distancing himself, and the barrels were sealed.

Its measure is for him to bore a hole, seal it, and dry it - If the Jew remained away for enough time for the gentile to bore a hole in the barrel's stopper, and then reseal the hole, and for the sealing to dry, the wine is forbidden.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says - The wine is not forbidden unless the Jew remains away for enough time for the gentile to open the entire stopper of the barrel, and it is impossible to remove the stopper without breaking it completely.
And stop it - and the gentile makes another new stopper.

And dry - and the stopper dries, but for boring a hole, the Sages were not concerned because it is noticeable. And shetom is like the expression shetom ha'ayin (Numbers 24:3), an open eye that sees well.

Wine left in a place where a gentile is present and a Jew enters at every moment.
Wine is permitted, even if a Jew left a gentile alone in the place where the liquid is located, whether in a store, on a vessel, or in a wagon; the Jew may even be absent to go to the synagogue or any house. The same applies when a gentile transported a barrel of wine from one place to another during the absence of the Jew, who left the gentile alone where the wine was.
GLOSS: It is forbidden to deliberately leave wine or vinegar in a gentile's house if the gentile lives alone; but if it has already happened, the wine is permitted. The wine is also permitted when the transport occurred during the absence of the Jew who had entrusted its custody to a gentile, because the latter fears the sudden arrival of the Jew. In all cases, one must be unaware of what the gentile may have done, i.e., whether he closed the door or moved the wagon or vessel to hide from view.
The wine is also permitted, even if the gentile closed the door of the store, if it has a crack or a hole allowing one to see everything that happens inside; this case is assimilated to that of an open door. The wine is permitted only if there is a roundabout path that allows the Jew to return suddenly, without the gentile being able to see him; the same applies when the Jew went to the bathhouse. When the Jew entered a bathhouse, to the knowledge of the gentile, who then knows perfectly well that the Jew will be absent for a long time; or when the Jew told the gentile: «Guard the wine in my store», because the gentile then understood that the Jew was to go away; or when he told the gentile: «Transport the barrel of wine to such and such a place, I will return afterwards»; when the Jew announced to the gentile that he was separating from him, all barrels of wine are forbidden if they are open; if they are sealed, and if the Jew went far enough away to give the gentile time to open them and close them with clay or lime and make any trace of moisture disappear, they are all forbidden.
GLOSS: Some authors claim that wine contained in closed and sealed barrels is always permitted, because one seal is sufficient for a barrel of wine; this opinion can be accepted when the loss caused by the prohibition would be significant.

With regard to one who placed his wine in a wagon or on a ship with a gentile, and went on his way by a shortcut [bekappendarya], such that the gentile does not know when the Jew will encounter the gentile, even if the Jew entered the city and bathed, the wine is permitted, because the gentile would not use the wine for a libation, for fear the owner might catch the gentile at it.
One who placed his wine in a wagon or on a ship - with the gentile.
And went - the Jew by a shortcut.
And entered the city and bathed - in the bathhouse, the wine is permitted, since the gentile did not know that the Jew was delayed, the gentile was afraid and did not touch the wine.

If the Jew informed the gentile that the Jew was going away for a long period of time, the wine is forbidden if it was sufficient time for the gentile to bore a hole in the barrel, seal it again with plaster, and for the plaster to dry. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: It is forbidden only if it was sufficient time for the gentile to open the barrel by removing the stopper altogether, stop the barrel again, and for the new stopper to dry.

With regard to one who left a gentile in the Jew's shop, even if the Jew went out and came in and was not there all the time, the wine is permitted. But if the Jew informed the gentile that the Jew was going away for a long period of time, the wine is forbidden if it was sufficient time for the gentile to bore a hole in the barrel, seal it again with plaster, and for the plaster to dry. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: The wine is forbidden only if it was sufficient time for the gentile to open the barrel, stop the barrel again, and for the new stopper to dry.

If a Jew was eating with a gentile at the table, and left jugs [laginin] of wine on the table and a jug on the side table [hadulebaki], and the Jew left the gentile and went out, what is on the table is forbidden, as it is likely that the gentile handled the wine, whereas what is on the side table is permitted. But if the Jew said to the gentile: Mix water with the wine and the gentile may drink, even the jug that is on the side table is forbidden. Similarly, open barrels are forbidden, but sealed barrels are permitted unless the Jew was out of the room for sufficient time for the gentile to open the barrel by removing the stopper, and stop the barrel again by making a new stopper, and for the new stopper to dry.
What is on the table is forbidden - because the gentile will say: This Jew invited me to eat and drink, and the gentile touched the wine.
What is on the side table is permitted - because it is not prepared for this meal.
And if he said to him: Mix and drink - Since the Jew strengthened the gentile's hands with some permission, the gentile's mind is at ease, and the gentile touched all of the wine.
Open barrels - in the house are forbidden.

Sealed barrels are permitted - until the Jew remains away for enough time for the gentile to open, stop, and dry, and the anonymous Mishna follows Rabban Shimon since it does not state 'to bore a hole'.

When a Jew and a gentile are sitting and each drinking their own wine, when the former hears that he is being called to go to the synagogue; he goes to pray and leaves his wine there: it remains permitted, if there is a roundabout path allowing the Jew to unexpectedly return to the place where he left the gentile. But if the wine remained on the table, while another wine was placed at a certain distance from the furniture, the first is forbidden if the gentile remained alone; the second is also forbidden, if it was placed within reach of the gentile's hand; but it is permitted, if the distance separating it from the gentile did not allow the latter to touch it by extending his hand. When a Jew told a gentile to mix water with wine to make a drink, all barrels filled with this liquid, which were in the house and were open, are forbidden; those that were closed are permitted, provided, however, that the gentile did not remain alone for a long enough time to allow him to open and close the barrels with clay or lime and make any trace of moisture disappear.
